transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Sanjay Patel (Redwood AE), Elena Ruiz (Redwood SE), Maya Lin (Verdant Data - Head of ML), Tom Reynolds (Verdant - CTO), Aisha Khan (Verdant - Platform Eng)

Summary:
Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming, key params (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retries/idempotency, and integration considerations. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated (cost & latency tradeoffs) and needs perf benchmarks on their prompt set. Security/compliance questions surfaced but mostly around encryption at rest, audit logs, and data retention.

Topics covered:
- Hosted API capabilities (chat, text generation, streaming)
- Request params and effects on output / cost
- Retries, idempotency, and error handling patterns
- Rate limits, backoff, and recommended SDK patterns
- Observability: Console metrics, token-level cost breakdowns
- Next steps: share pricing, run benchmark, provide prompts

Transcript:
[00:00] Speaker 1 (Sanjay): Hey everyone thanks for joining, we got about 40 minutes together, do you want to do quick intros?
[00:06] Speaker 2 (Maya): Yeah Maya here, head of ML at Verdant Data, Tom is our CTO and Aisha runs infra.
[00:10] Speaker 3 (Tom): hi all, thanks for setting up.
[00:12] Speaker 1 (Sanjay): Great, I'll hand to Elena for a quick demo of the hosted API, focusing on chat and text gen basics.
[00:17] Speaker 4 (Elena): cool, so I'm going to share a short demo, link to the deck in the chat: https://redwood.app/decks/hosted-api-demo, and i'll show streaming, params like temperature and top_p, and how we recommend handling retries.
[00:35] Speaker 4 (Elena): first demo, simple chat completion call. We use the /v1/chat/completions endpoint, messages array, model selection. Note: our hosted catalog has curated models and performance profiles; for low-latency interactive use we recommend the smaller open models or our optimized variants.
[01:02] Speaker 2 (Maya): quick q: can you stream partial tokens? we need UI to start rendering asap.
[01:06] Speaker 4 (Elena): yes, streaming is supported. We'll send chunks via SSE or websockets in the SDKs. You get incremental tokens and also a final delta event. Keep in mind streaming increases the number of small network calls but lowers TTFI (time to first token).
[01:30] Speaker 4 (Elena): demo snippet: set stream=true, set max_tokens to bound cost, set temperature 0.2 for deterministic results, or 0.8 if you want more creative output. We also recommend top_p for nucleus sampling when you need fine control.
[01:55] Speaker 3 (Tom): are temp/top_p and max_tokens the main levers for output diversity and cost?
[02:00] Speaker 4 (Elena): correct. temperature/top_p affect randomness, max_tokens directly controls token volume and cost. Also presence_penalty/frequency_penalty if you need to reduce repetition.
[02:20] Speaker 2 (Maya): on retries, we have transient network issues inside our VPC, what's the recommended pattern?
[02:24] Speaker 4 (Elena): good question. Use idempotency keys for any stateful requests; for stateless chat completions we recommend a deterministic client-side nonce if you want repeatability. For retries: exponential backoff with jitter, and only retry on 5xx or connection errors, not 4xx. For streaming requests, if a connection drops you can resume from KV-cache using the message prefix — though for hosted we surface resumable tokens on some models.
[03:05] Speaker 1 (Sanjay): to add, our SDKs have built-in retry middleware that follows these best practices and logs retry counts to the console.
[03:20] Speaker 4 (Elena): also covering rate limiting: hosted API has per-account rate limits; if you hit a 429 we provide a Retry-After header. For higher throughput we recommend Redwood Dedicated or reserved capacity.
[03:45] Speaker 3 (Tom): approx latency numbers? for our use case we want sub-400ms median for short prompts.
[03:51] Speaker 4 (Elena): it depends on model and seq length. For small models in hosted we see 80-250ms for 16-32 token responses; for larger context or autoregressive long outputs latency increases. We can run a benchmark on your actual prompts and provide percentiles.
[04:10] Speaker 2 (Maya): okay, send benchmark pls. Also curious about cost — token pricing and how streaming affects billing.
[04:17] Speaker 1 (Sanjay): billing is per-output token for generation and per-input token for embeddings; streaming doesn't change token counts, it's only more network interactions. We'll include token cost examples in the pricing deck.
[04:40] Speaker 4 (Elena): demo: show console - per-route cost breakdown, token-level insights, latency histograms, and tracing hooks. Quick note: you can set per-route model pins and routing policies.
[05:05] Speaker 2 (Maya): security — we are regulated, need SOC2, data retention controls, KMS, and audit logs.
[05:10] Speaker 1 (Sanjay): we have SOC 2 Type II, customer-managed KMS for Private deployments and Keywrap options for Hosted; audit logs and retention controls are available - we'll share the security whitepaper.
[05:30] Speaker 3 (Tom): what about data residency? some data must remain in EU.
[05:33] Speaker 1 (Sanjay): hosted can be region-scoped; we have EU regions and can sign data residency clauses for enterprise contracts; Dedicated/Private gives you more control if you need strict residency.
[06:00] Speaker 4 (Elena): switching back to the API - here's an example of structured output and function calling, you can ask the model to return JSON objects and we provide schema hints to improve parsing.
[06:26] Speaker 2 (Maya): does that increase hallucinations?
[06:28] Speaker 4 (Elena): function-calling often reduces hallucinations because you constrain the response shape; still need evals and prompt engineering. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization/profile changes if you prioritize cost.
[06:50] Speaker 1 (Sanjay): a likely flow: start with hosted to iterate quickly, then if you need predictable latency or throughput commit to Dedicated.
[07:02] Speaker 3 (Tom): what about retry semantics for streaming responses? you said resumable tokens — can you explain again?
[07:06] Speaker 4 (Elena): sure, resumable streaming is model-dependent. We keep a short-lived KV cache for active sessions that maps prefixes to cache keys. If the connection drops, you can resend with the cache key to resume from last returned token. It's not guaranteed for all models, but it's supported for our optimized variants.
[07:45] Speaker 2 (Maya): hmm ok, interesting — for our front-end we want minimal flicker.
[07:50] Speaker 4 (Elena): we also recommend server-side buffering and re-assembling chunks to reduce UI flicker, plus heuristics to switch to final text if latency exceeds a threshold.
[08:10] Speaker 1 (Sanjay): let's talk error codes quickly — 4xx indicates client error, 401 for auth, 403 for permission, 429 rate limits, 503/500 server errors are retryable, and 499 if client closed connection.
[08:28] Speaker 3 (Tom): how does authentication work?
[08:31] Speaker 4 (Elena): standard API keys for hosted; for enterprise we support mTLS and SSO integrations for the Console. We also have fine-grained RBAC in the Console.
[08:50] Speaker 2 (Maya): can we throttle by user? e.g., per-customer usage in our product so no single user spikes cost?
[08:55] Speaker 1 (Sanjay): yes you can implement per-user quotas on your side; we can also set per-route quotas and limits to help.
[09:12] Speaker 4 (Elena): demo - code sample showing retries: exponential backoff with max attempts, log error details to the console, and surface model_version in the response to help debugging after a rollback.
[09:40] Speaker 2 (Maya): model version pinning is critical for us so we don't get regressions in output quality.
[09:44] Speaker 1 (Sanjay): absolutely, we support version pinning and rollout policies (canary, A/B) in the Console. We'll show an example in the documentation.
[10:00] Speaker 4 (Elena): now quick Q&A from the demo — one sec, i'm pulling up sample prompt tests.
[10:12] Speaker 2 (Maya): we have a prompt set that is multi-turn and has few-shot examples; how do you recommend batching these?
[10:16] Speaker 4 (Elena): batching works best server-side for high throughput workloads — Redwood's runtime supports continuous batching and prefix cache to avoid re-computing the few-shot context for every request. For interactive low-latency flows, avoid large batch delays; use small micro-batches or single requests.
[10:45] Speaker 3 (Tom): do you support token-level streaming metrics so we can estimate cost on incomplete responses?
[10:49] Speaker 4 (Elena): we expose token counts per request in realtime in the console and via webhooks. That lets you approximate cost before finalization.
[11:10] Speaker 2 (Maya): practical concern — our traffic is spiky; what's the burst model?
[11:14] Speaker 1 (Sanjay): hosted has configurable burst limits; if your needs are predictable then Dedicated with reserved capacity is the best fit to keep latency SLOs. We can also support scheduled warmers for predictable spikes.
[11:35] Speaker 2 (Maya): can we run a short PoC on hosted with a trial quota?
[11:38] Speaker 1 (Sanjay): yes, we'll add trial credits to your account and provide a demo token. I'll send details.
[11:50] Speaker 4 (Elena): another note on retries: avoid re-sending the same prompt blindly; if you get partial output, use the delta tokens and the resume key as mentioned.
[12:05] Speaker 2 (Maya): curious, do you provide any built-in prompt evaluation or quality regression tooling?
[12:09] Speaker 4 (Elena): yes, Redwood Optimize offers evals tied to prompt sets, regression alerts, and suggestions for quantization/model swap recommendations to balance cost vs quality.
[12:30] Speaker 3 (Tom): i want the perf numbers for our prompt set and the pricing to decide between hosted and dedicated.
[12:35] Speaker 1 (Sanjay): understood — we'll run the benchmark and include a cost/perf comparison.
[13:00] Speaker 2 (Maya): one more on compliance — can we configure retention to drop raw prompts after 30 days?
[13:05] Speaker 1 (Sanjay): yes, retention policies are configurable, and we can set shorter retention for sensitive data. For fully regulated workloads Private deployment with on-prem options is recommended.
[13:28] Speaker 4 (Elena): showing an example error trace in Console — you can see the request_id, model_version, and token counts; this helps debug misbehaving prompts.
[13:55] Speaker 2 (Maya): ok that's useful.
[14:05] Speaker 1 (Sanjay): quick recap: we'll send pricing + security docs, Elena will run perf tests on their prompts, and Verdant will share prompt set and traffic shape.
[14:20] Speaker 3 (Tom): timeline for decision? we hope to decide in 3-4 weeks.
[14:24] Speaker 1 (Sanjay): sounds good. We'll target the benchmark results within a week, and pricing follow-up the next day.
[14:35] Speaker 2 (Maya): thanks everyone, looking forward to the trial.
[14:38] Speaker 4 (Elena): thanks, i'll follow up with the benchmark plan.
[14:42] Speaker 1 (Sanjay): meeting adjourned.
